items.stem: Explain why Shakespeare's language had to create setting and time of day.
items.answer: Plays were performed in daylight with few props, so words like "what light through yonder window breaks" had to make the audience imagine night and place.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Plays were performed in daylight with few props, so words like "what light through yonder window breaks" had to make the audience imagine night and place. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Shakespeare's plays were written only for wealthy people." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The Globe's audience included groundlings who paid a penny to stand, so plays had to appeal to all classes with action, humour and spectacle.
items.markingKey: The Globe's audience included groundlings who paid a penny to stand, so plays had to appeal to all classes with action, humour and spectacle. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from Act 3 Scene 1 of Romeo and Juliet by William Shakespeare.

(TYBALT, under ROMEO's arm, stabs MERCUTIO, and flies with his followers.)
MERCUTIO: I am hurt.
A plague o' both your houses! I am sped.
ROMEO: Courage, man; the hurt cannot be much.
MERCUTIO: No, 'tis not so deep as a well, nor so wide as a church-door; but 'tis enough, 'twill serve: ask for me to-morrow, and you shall find me a grave man.

Explain how the Elizabethan context helps us understand this extract.
items.answer: Elizabethan audiences enjoyed sword fights on stage; the line "A plague o' both your houses!" would have had extra force at a time when outbreaks of plague often closed London's theatres.
items.markingKey: Elizabethan audiences enjoyed sword fights on stage; the line "A plague o' both your houses!" would have had extra force at a time when outbreaks of plague often closed London's theatres. Award marks for an accurate, specific point supported by a reference to the text (criterion A). A general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Explain how a groundling and a wealthy spectator might each enjoy the fight scene in Act 3 Scene 1.
items.answer: Groundlings would enjoy the sword fight and Mercutio's jokes; wealthy spectators might appreciate the wordplay (the "grave man" pun) and the tragic turning point.
items.markingKey: Groundlings would enjoy the sword fight and Mercutio's jokes; wealthy spectators might appreciate the wordplay (the "grave man" pun) and the tragic turning point.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Romeo and Juliet is more about fate than about the characters' own choices."
items.answer: Shakespeare balances the two: fate frames the story, but characters' impulsive choices and the adults' hatred cause the tragedy.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the Prologue calls them "star-cross'd"; coincidences such as the undelivered letter. Arguments against: Romeo kills Tybalt in anger; the feud and rushed marriage are human decisions. Supported judgement: Shakespeare balances the two: fate frames the story, but characters' impulsive choices and the adults' hatred cause the tragedy.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from Act 2 Scene 2 of Romeo and Juliet by William Shakespeare.

ROMEO:
But, soft! what light through yonder window breaks?
It is the east, and Juliet is the sun.
Arise, fair sun, and kill the envious moon,
Who is already sick and pale with grief,
That thou her maid art far more fair than she:

How does Shakespeare's use of verse contribute to the effect of this extract?
items.answer: Blank verse – unrhymed iambic pentameter ("It IS the EAST, and JU-liet IS the SUN") – gives Romeo's speech a dignified, heartbeat-like rhythm.

How does Shakespeare use the Prologue to prepare the audience for a tragedy?
Write one analytical paragraph (point, evidence, explanation) that answers this question, using at least two quotations.
items.answer: The Prologue is a formal sonnet in iambic pentameter spoken by the Chorus, which signals a serious, structured story. It reveals the outcome, creating dramatic irony. Wordplay on "civil" shows violence corrupting a civilised city, alliteration in "fatal ... foes" stresses doom, and "star-cross'd lovers" draws on Elizabethan beliefs about fate, telling the audience the lovers are destined to die.

Read the following description of a horror film trailer.

0:00 – Black screen. A child's music box plays slowly.
0:05 – Bright, sunny shots: a family moves into a farmhouse. Upbeat guitar.
0:15 – The music box again, louder. Quick cuts: a door swinging shut; a shadow on the stairs; the daughter staring at a wall.
0:25 – Silence. Close-up: the daughter turns to camera. "She says we can stay... if we're quiet."
0:28 – A crash of sound. Title: HUSH. In cinemas October.

Explain how camera and sound choices in this script create meaning.
items.answer: Editing moves from slow, sunny shots to rapid quick cuts, increasing pace and anxiety. Sound shifts from upbeat guitar to a distorted music box, then sudden silence and a crash (a jump scare). The close-up of the daughter speaking to camera breaks the fourth wall and unsettles the viewer.

items.answer: playscript extract

items.stem: Distinguish between dramatic irony and situational irony.
items.answer: Dramatic irony is when the audience knows more than the characters (we know the lovers will die); situational irony is when the outcome is the opposite of what is expected (Romeo's attempt at peace leads to Mercutio's death).
items.markingKey: Dramatic irony is when the audience knows more than the characters (we know the lovers will die); situational irony is when the outcome is the opposite of what is expected (Romeo's attempt at peace leads to Mercutio's death). items.stem: Explain the difference between a modernised adaptation and a traditional adaptation.
items.answer: A traditional adaptation keeps the original period and setting (Zeffirelli's Renaissance Verona); a modernised one moves the story to a contemporary setting (Luhrmann's Verona Beach) to highlight its relevance.

items.stem: Explain why Shakespeare makes Romeo and Juliet's first conversation a sonnet.
items.answer: The sonnet is the form of love poetry, so sharing one shows their instant connection and harmony.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: The sonnet is the form of love poetry, so sharing one shows their instant connection and harmony. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why the Elizabethan audience's beliefs about fate matter to Romeo and Juliet.
items.answer: Many believed destiny was written in the stars, so the Prologue's "star-cross'd" lovers would seem genuinely doomed, increasing tragic tension.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Many believed destiny was written in the stars, so the Prologue's "star-cross'd" lovers would seem genuinely doomed, increasing tragic tension. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Briefly explain why Mercutio's death changes the mood of the play.
items.answer: It removes the play's main source of comedy and provokes Romeo's revenge, turning romance into tragedy.

Read the following extract from Act 3 Scene 1 of Romeo and Juliet by William Shakespeare.

(TYBALT, under ROMEO's arm, stabs MERCUTIO, and flies with his followers.)
MERCUTIO: I am hurt.
A plague o' both your houses! I am sped.
ROMEO: Courage, man; the hurt cannot be much.
MERCUTIO: No, 'tis not so deep as a well, nor so wide as a church-door; but 'tis enough, 'twill serve: ask for me to-morrow, and you shall find me a grave man.

How might a modern film adaptation stage this extract differently from a traditional one? Give two examples.
items.answer: Mercutio's death at the centre of the play: it is the turning point (peripeteia) that shifts the play from romance to tragedy.

items.stem:
Read the following extract from the Prologue of Romeo and Juliet by William Shakespeare (c. 1595).

CHORUS:
Two households, both alike in dignity,
In fair Verona, where we lay our scene,
From ancient grudge break to new mutiny,
Where civil blood makes civil hands unclean.
From forth the fatal loins of these two foes
A pair of star-cross'd lovers take their life;

How does Shakespeare's use of verse contribute to the effect of this extract?
items.answer: The lines are in iambic pentameter: five pairs of unstressed-stressed syllables ("Two HOUSE-holds, BOTH a-LIKE in DIG-ni-TY"), giving a formal, rhythmic voice suited to a Chorus introducing a tragedy.
items.markingKey: The lines are in iambic pentameter: five pairs of unstressed-stressed syllables ("Two HOUSE-holds, BOTH a-LIKE in DIG-ni-TY"), giving a formal, rhythmic voice suited to a Chorus introducing a tragedy. items.stem: Rafael writes: "Shakespeare's plays were written only for wealthy people." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: The Globe's audience included groundlings who paid a penny to stand, so plays had to appeal to all classes with action, humour and spectacle.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Shakespeare's language is a barrier for modern students."
items.answer: The language is challenging but rewarding; performance, glosses and close reading reveal how its rhythm and imagery still create meaning.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: old vocabulary and syntax; puns that are hard to understand. Arguments against: performance and context make meaning clear; many phrases are still used today; the imagery remains powerful. Supported judgement: The language is challenging but rewarding; performance, glosses and close reading reveal how its rhythm and imagery still create meaning.

items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Romeo and Juliet is more about fate than about the characters' own choices."
items.answer: Shakespeare balances the two: fate frames the story, but characters' impulsive choices and the adults' hatred cause the tragedy.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: the Prologue calls them "star-cross'd"; coincidences such as the undelivered letter. Arguments against: Romeo kills Tybalt in anger; the feud and rushed marriage are human decisions. Supported judgement: Shakespeare balances the two: fate frames the story, but characters' impulsive choices and the adults' hatred cause the tragedy. items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Mercutio's death is the most important moment in the play."
items.answer: Mercutio's death is the structural turning point, though its importance depends on the events it connects – the love before and the tragedy after.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: it turns comedy into tragedy; it causes Romeo's banishment. Arguments against: the lovers' meeting or the final deaths are equally crucial; the Prologue shapes the whole play.
